segments.say: So let's step back and look at the whole night. We began with a simple puzzle: how can a dream feel exactly as real as being awake, and then turn out to be nothing at all? We have followed that question through the sleeping brain, and we have met studies, doubts and a few surprises. Now it is time to gather what is worth keeping.

show.title: What it all adds up to

segments.say: Here is the first thing to carry with you. A dream is a world that your brain builds, even though your eyes are closed and the room is dark. The researcher Antti Revonsuo, in a paper published in 2000, described the dreaming brain as producing a complex model of the world. That is the same kind of work it does all day, and it is why a dream can feel like life, right up to the moment you wake.

Maquet and his colleagues scanned seven people during REM sleep. They found that blood flow rose in areas linked to emotion, such as the amygdala, and fell in a large part of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, a region involved in careful thinking. In plain terms, the feeling machinery was busy while some of the judging machinery was quiet.

show.what: Functional neuroanatomy of human rapid-eye-movement sleep and dreaming

segments.say: That is the second thing to carry with you. The oddness of dreams, the sudden changes of place and the people who are two people at once, may be what a quieter prefrontal cortex feels like from the inside. You do not stop to question it, because the part of you that would question it is resting. It is not a flaw in you. It is simply how this state of the brain works.

Four small ideas, then. None of them asks you to do anything, or to change anything. They are simply a gentler way to think about the odd theatre that runs every night inside your head, and about the mornings when it leaves nothing behind.

show.title: What to take with you
items: A dream is the brain building a world
The strangeness comes from a quieter judging brain
A few words, soon after waking, can keep a thread

segments.say: It is worth saying again that nobody needs to remember their dreams. The research we looked at suggests that people who recall more tend to wake briefly more often, and to differ a little in how their brains attend to the world. That is a difference, and not a prize. Your dreams do their quiet work, whether or not you ever carry them into the morning.

show.sub: You do not have to remember

segments.say: But if you are curious, there is a kind and simple practice. Keep a notebook within reach, and when you wake, lie still for a moment and ask yourself what was just happening. Write down a place, a person, a feeling, only a few words. The studies were honest that a diary is no magic trick, and that it can feel like homework. So keep it light, and let it stay a pleasure.

A small light and a notebook, nothing more. That is all a dream diary needs to be. Some people fill pages with it, and others write a single word and are content. Either way, it is a way of saying to the night that you were paying attention, and that you are glad of whatever it gave you.

Do you remember where we started? That moment of waking with your heart racing, sure that something terrible, or wonderful, had just happened. Now you know a little about why. Your brain had built a world, and its emotional machinery had been fully awake inside it, while the part that checks and doubts had been quiet. Your heart was responding to something that felt real, even though it never was.

It helps to know that, the next time it happens. A racing heart after a dream is not a warning, and it is not a sign that something is wrong with you. It is the body following the story that the brain was telling, a little behind, as the world of the dream falls away. You can take a slow breath, feel the room come back, and let the feeling settle.

Here, in the briefest outline, is where we have been. A strange eye movement was seen in sleeping people, and a whole science grew from it. Dreaming turned out to be wider than REM, the dream world turned out to be built from the same machinery as the waking one, and forgetting turned out to be the usual ending. Thank you for coming along.

show.title: The night, in review
items: Dreams can happen outside REM too
The brain builds a world, and a quiet prefrontal cortex accepts it
Dreams fade, and that is normal

segments.say: And now, if you would like to, let the thinking go quiet. You have done enough of it for one night. What follows is only for resting, so there is nothing to remember, and nothing to get right.
Allow your shoulders to be heavier than they were a moment ago, and let your hands rest wherever they are, without any need to hold on to anything at all.

Notice the weight of your head, and the way the surface beneath you holds it so easily, as it has done on countless other nights. There is nothing you need to solve, and nothing that must be finished before morning, because the day has done what it could and it can stay where it is.

Let your breathing go on in its own time, a little slower with each breath, and do not try to steer it. Each time you breathe out, let some of the day leave with it, the small worries, the half-finished thoughts, the sentences you meant to say.

They will keep, and they will be waiting if you want them tomorrow. But for now, there is only the quiet rhythm of the breath, rising and falling, rising and falling, like a tide that has no need to hurry.

Picture a small room with a low fire, and a soft glow that moves slowly on the walls. The air in the room is warm and still, and the sound of it is only the faint crackle of a log settling into its place.
Nothing in this room asks anything of you, and you are welcome to stay for as long as you like. The light is gentle, the shadows are soft, and everything here is exactly as it should be.
Now let the feeling of heaviness spread, from your forehead down through your cheeks, your jaw, your neck, and into your arms, so that they feel like warm sand.

Let it travel through your chest and your stomach, down through your legs and your feet, until your whole body is resting, easily and completely, as if you were sinking an inch or two into the softness beneath you. There is no need to move, and no need to try.

Imagine a lake, so still that the stars lie upon it as clearly as they hang in the sky. There is no wind, and no sound, except perhaps the far-off call of a bird, so soft that you barely hear it. You are standing at the edge, in no hurry, and the air is cool and clean. Everything is quiet, and everything is at peace.

If a thought drifts in, you can let it float by, like a cloud crossing a night sky, and you need not follow it anywhere. Another one will come and go in its own time, and each one will be a little softer and a little further away. There is no need to push anything out, or to hold anything in. The mind, left alone, settles by itself, in the way the lake does when the breeze has died.

Tonight, your brain will begin its slow cycles again, and somewhere in them it may build a world for you. It may be a gentle one or a strange one, and you will know a little more now about why it feels so real. You do not have to steer it, or to remember it, or to explain it. You can simply let it be your brain's quiet work, done on your behalf while you rest.

If you wake in the night, with a faint feeling left over from a dream, there is nothing to be afraid of. It was a story that your own mind was telling, and it has finished now. You can feel the room around you, the cool air, the weight of the blanket, and the steady slow rhythm of your own breath, and you can drift down again, as gently as a leaf settling on still water.

Before you go, you might thank your brain for the long night's work, for the worlds it builds and the stories it tells, and for the way it keeps on doing both without ever being asked. It has been looking after you, in its strange and patient way, for every night of your life, and it will go on doing so tonight, whether you notice it or not. That, perhaps, is the most reassuring thing the research has to say: the work goes on quietly without you, and you are free to rest.

And so you let the last of the day go, and then the last of the night's thoughts as well, until there is just the warmth of the room, the softness beneath you and the slow, easy breath. Your eyes are heavy, and your mind is quiet, and you are ready, in your own time, to slip into the first slow cycle of sleep. There is no hurry at all, and whenever you drift off, it will be exactly the right moment.

Rest now, with nothing left to do and nowhere left to be, while the quiet gathers around you like a soft blanket. May your dreams be kind, and may they feel as real and as warm as they like, and may you wake tomorrow rested and unhurried, with the light coming gently into the room. Goodnight, and sleep well.

Thank you for spending this time with me, and for listening so patiently. If you enjoyed tonight, I would be glad to see you again soon, and I have something curious waiting for you: why you talk to yourself, and what that quiet voice is really doing. Until then, take good care, and sleep well.
